p: Jeremiah's home was a few miles from Jerusalem, in a town given to the priests.
b: Anathoth lay about three miles north-east of Jerusalem and was one of the towns given to the descendants of Aaron (Joshua 21:18). Many scholars connect Jeremiah's family with Abiathar, the priest whom Solomon sent home to his fields at Anathoth (1 Kings 2:26-27); the book never says this. His father's name, Hilkiah, is also the name of the high priest of Josiah's day (2 Kings 22:4). The book does not call them the same man, and since the high priests of Jerusalem came from Zadok's line, most scholars think they were different men. Jeremiah's own townsmen later plotted against him (11:21).

a: the thirteenth year of his rule
t: 627 BC and the long silence about Josiah
p: The call is dated to Josiah's thirteenth year, about 627 BC, five years before his reform.
b: Josiah became king in 640 BC, so his thirteenth year is 628/627. The book of Kings dates the finding of the law scroll and Josiah's reform to his eighteenth year, 622 (2 Kings 22:3). Strangely, Jeremiah never names the reform or the scroll. Scholars explain this in different ways: Jeremiah was silent for those years; the reform was only partly effective (3:10 says Judah returned only 'with a lie'); or the call is dated to a different year, which a few scholars propose. The headings in 1:1-3 are the book's editors' summary of a ministry of about forty years, from 627 to 586.

p: The ministry ends with the burning of Jerusalem in the fifth month.
b: The fifth month is Av, about July or August. The Temple was burned on the seventh to the tenth day of that month in the year 586 (2 Kings 25:8-9; Jeremiah 52:12-13). Jewish tradition fixes the fast of the Ninth of Av on this month, and the Talmud remembers the destruction of both Temples on that date (Mishnah Taanit 4:6). The 'eleventh year of Zedekiah' is the end of the line the book draws: Josiah, Jehoiakim and Zedekiah, with Jehoahaz and Jehoiachin (who reigned only three months each) left out.

p: The Plain English Translation writes the divine name YHWH as 'the LORD', in capitals.
b: As in most English Bibles, 'the LORD' stands for the Hebrew name YHWH, which was not read aloud in later Jewish custom; readers said Adonai ('my Lord') instead. 'The Lord GOD' (first in 1:6) is Adonai YHWH. In Jeremiah the formula 'The word of the LORD came to me' (1:4, 11, 13) opens many messages, and the book often adds that the name is God's own: 'they will know that my name is the LORD' (16:21). Jeremiah's own name probably means 'the LORD lifts up' or 'the LORD throws', in either case with the divine name as its last syllable.

t: To know, to shape, to make holy
p: 'Know' here means to choose and care for; 'shape' is a potter's verb.
b: Three verbs describe the LORD's work. Yada', 'know', means more than awareness: it is the word for a chosen, close relationship (Genesis 18:19; Amos 3:2; Hosea 13:5). Yatsar, 'shape', is a potter's word (Genesis 2:7; Isaiah 44:2, 24). Hiqdashtikha, 'I made you holy', means set apart for the LORD's use. The language is close to the calls of the Servant in Isaiah 49:1, 5, and Paul uses it of himself (Galatians 1:15). The manuscripts spell 'I shaped you' in two ways, a matter of spelling only.
r: Isaiah 49:1; Isaiah 49:5; Psalm 139:13-16; Galatians 1:15; Luke 1:15; Judges 13:5

a: Before I shaped you in the belly
p: The verse is about God choosing a prophet; churches use it in debates on the unborn.
b: A popular belief says this verse defines when a person's life begins. The verse does not say that. It tells how the LORD set apart one man, Jeremiah, for a work before he was born. Its subject is God's knowing and calling (see the note on 'I knew you'), and its verb for the womb is the potter's yatsar, 'shape', not a word for conception. It is still used in debates on the unborn. The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes it, with Psalm 139 in its notes, among its signs that human life is to be protected from conception (2270). The Presbyterian Church in America's 1978 committee report on abortion cites it to show God's personal involvement with a child before birth. Many Jewish readers, and some Christian ones, take it as proof only of God's foreknowledge of a prophet. Rashi dates God's knowing of Jeremiah to the days of Adam, and says 'prophet to the nations' may mean a prophet to Israel that acts like the nations. The card below sets out how churches use it.
r: Psalm 139:13-16; Isaiah 49:1; Galatians 1:15; Luke 1:41-44; Judges 13:5-7; Deuteronomy 18:18

p: Like Moses and Gideon, Jeremiah first says he is not the man.
b: Na'ar, 'boy' or 'youth', does not give an age: it can be a child (1 Samuel 1:24; 2 Kings 2:23) or a young man (Genesis 41:12). Prophets and leaders in the Bible often protest at their call: Moses says he is slow of speech (Exodus 4:10), Gideon that his clan is the weakest (Judges 6:15), Isaiah that his lips are unclean (Isaiah 6:5). In each case the LORD answers with a promise of his presence and a touch or sign. Jeremiah's answer, 'I am with you' (1:8, 19), is the same promise given to Moses (Exodus 3:12).

p: The Hebrew ne'um YHWH is a spoken oracle formula.
b: Ne'um YHWH is a noun phrase, 'an utterance of the LORD'. Jeremiah uses it well over a hundred times, most often at the end of a sentence, as here. It marks the words as an oracle, spoken by the LORD himself and not just reported. The Plain English Translation sets it off with commas and keeps it as 'the LORD declares', and the opening 'The LORD says this' (koh amar YHWH, first at 2:2) is the formula a messenger used when he delivered a king's words.

t: Words put in a prophet's mouth
p: The LORD's touch recalls Isaiah's lips and the promise of a prophet like Moses.
b: The LORD's words to Jeremiah, 'I have set my words in your mouth', are the language of the promise in Deuteronomy 18:18: 'I will raise up for them a prophet like you ... and I will put my words in his mouth.' The book presents Jeremiah as that kind of prophet. The touch on the lips is also like the burning coal that touched Isaiah (Isaiah 6:6-7), and the scroll that Ezekiel was told to eat (Ezekiel 2:8-3:3). Later the LORD says, 'I am making the words in your mouth into fire' (5:14).

a: to pull up and pull down, to destroy and demolish, to build and to plant
p: Four verbs of ruin and two of rebuilding sum up the book.
b: Jeremiah's task has six verbs, four of ruin and two of renewal, and the book returns to them: 12:14-17; 18:7-10; 24:6; 31:28; 42:10; 45:4. The first two verbs rhyme in Hebrew, linthosh ulinthots: nathash is pulling up a plant by the roots, nathats is breaking down a wall. The prophet is 'over the nations', which fits 1:5 and the oracles against the nations in 46-51, and 'over the kingdoms', not only Judah. The balance matters: judgment comes first, but it is not the last word.

p: A play on two Hebrew words, shaqed 'almond' and shoqed 'watching'.
b: The almond (shaqed) is the first tree to bloom in the Judean winter, usually in January, so its name could be heard as 'the wakeful one'. In the next verse the LORD says he is shoqed, 'watching' or 'staying awake', over his word. English cannot keep the pun, so the Plain English Translation gives the Hebrew in this note. Jerome did it in Latin by reading the first as 'a watching rod' (virgam vigilantem). Compare Amos 8:1-2, where a basket of summer fruit (qayits) announces 'the end' (qets). The Greek translator saw 'a rod of a nut tree' and lost the play.

a: a pot with the fire fanned under it
p: A pot on a blown fire tips its face away from the north.
b: Sir naphuach is a pot on a fire that someone is blowing on, so it is boiling or about to boil over. Where it faces is not clear. 'Its face is away from the north' can mean that the lip is tilted so that the contents will pour out toward the south, as most readers take it, or that the pot sits in the north and faces us. Ezekiel used a boiling pot for Jerusalem under siege (Ezekiel 11:3-11; 24:3-14), where the city is the pot. Here the pot is the north, and Judah is where it spills.

t: Who is the foe from the north?
p: Scythians, Babylonians or a mythic enemy: the book never names the foe in these chapters.
b: Who comes from the north is a famous puzzle. (1) Scythians. Herodotus (Histories 1.103-106) tells of horsemen from the steppe who swept through Asia and reached the border of Egypt in Josiah's time, and many 19th-century scholars read these poems as about them. No Scythian attack on Judah has been found in the record, and many scholars now doubt the story. (2) Babylon, the empire that did destroy Jerusalem; chapter 25:9 names 'all the clans of the north' and Nebuchadnezzar together. On this view the poems were written or reshaped after Babylon rose. (3) A mythic enemy: Brevard Childs argued that 'the north' recalls the home of the gods' enemies in Israel's old traditions, so the language was already traditional before any army was named. The LORD himself calls the foe (1:15; 4:6; 5:15).
r: Jeremiah 4:6; Jeremiah 6:22; Jeremiah 25:9; Jeremiah 46:20; Psalm 48:2; Isaiah 14:13

a: set his throne at the opening of Jerusalem's gates
p: The city gate was where kings sat to judge; here the invaders sit in judgment.
b: The gate of an ancient city was its court and meeting place. Kings and elders sat there to give judgment (Ruth 4:1-2; Proverbs 31:23). The northern kings will put their thrones in the gateway, which means they will try Jerusalem and pass sentence, as the LORD's 'rulings' in the next verse also say. The picture came true: when Jerusalem was breached, the Babylonian officers 'sat in the Middle Gate' (39:3). The 'clans of the northern kingdoms' fits the Babylonian army, which drew on many peoples under Nebuchadnezzar.

p: Mishpatim are court sentences, the verdict that follows the charge.
b: Mishpatim here are judicial rulings or sentences. The language is a courtroom: the LORD states the charge (they left me, burned incense to other gods, worshiped what their hands made) and will 'speak' the sentence 'with' them, as a judge does with an accused person. The same word describes God's rulings in the law, so the verdict is based on the covenant. The charge is the first commandments: no other gods and no images (Exodus 20:3-5). 'The work of their own hands' is the standard Bible phrase for idols (Deuteronomy 4:28; Isaiah 2:8).

a: Do not break down before them
t: A warning with the same word twice
p: Hebrew uses one verb twice: do not be shattered, or I will shatter you.
b: Hatat means to be shattered or dismayed, and the verse uses the verb twice, 'do not be shattered before them, lest I shatter you before them'. The prophet's fear would make him useless; the LORD's answer is that fear would bring something worse. The Greek has no threat at all; it gives a promise (see the variant). 'Tie your belt tight' is the idiom 'gird up your loins': the long robe is tucked into the belt so that a man can run or work.

t: A city with walls of bronze
p: The soft young prophet becomes a fortress against the whole country.
b: A fortified city ('ir mivtsar), an iron pillar and bronze walls: three pictures of what cannot be broken. The LORD does not make Jeremiah safe from the people; he makes him strong enough to stand against them. Compare Ezekiel's forehead 'harder than flint' (Ezekiel 3:8-9) and the Servant's face 'like flint' (Isaiah 50:7). The promise returns in Jeremiah 15:20, after Jeremiah has complained and almost given up. Four groups stand against him: the kings, the officials, the priests and 'the people of the land' ('am ha'arets), a term that in Judah usually means the landowning citizens, who helped put kings on the throne (2 Kings 21:24; 23:30).

p: Jeremiah was beaten, jailed and dropped in a cistern, but he was not beaten in the end.
b: The promise is that the fighters will not 'prevail', not that there will be no fight. Jeremiah's neighbors plotted to kill him (11:18-23), the priest Pashhur had him beaten and put in the stocks (20:1-2), a mob seized him in the Temple (26:8), the officials threw him into a cistern (38:6), and in the end the Judeans in Egypt, who took him with them, did not listen to him (43:2-7). Yet Jerusalem fell as he had said, and he was freed by the Babylonians (39:11-14; 40:1-4). The promise is of survival, and of the truth of his word.

p: 'The LORD says this' is how a royal messenger started.
b: Koh amar YHWH, literally 'thus says the LORD', is the formula of a messenger who delivers his master's words: Jacob's servants say 'Thus says your servant Jacob' (Genesis 32:4), and Sennacherib's envoy 'Thus says the great king' (2 Kings 18:19). The prophet is the LORD's envoy, so what follows is the master's word, not his own. Jeremiah uses it well over a hundred times. The Plain English Translation renders it 'The LORD says this'; the formula that closes a message is 'the LORD declares' (1:8).

a: how you walked after me in the wilderness
p: The wilderness years are remembered as Israel's bridal days.
b: The LORD remembers Israel as a young bride who followed him through an unplanted land. This is the opposite of the picture in Numbers and Ezekiel, where the wilderness years are years of complaint (Numbers 14; Ezekiel 20:13). Hosea has the same hopeful picture: the LORD will lead Israel back into the wilderness and speak tenderly to her (Hosea 2:14-15; 9:10). Hesed, 'loyal love', is usually God's faithfulness; it is rare for Israel's (Hosea 6:4). The 'love of your engagement' (kelulot) means the bride's love in the days of betrothal, before the marriage.

p: Those who ate holy produce were guilty; those who 'devoured' Israel will be too.
b: Israel is pictured as the first share of a harvest, which belonged to the LORD (Exodus 23:19; Deuteronomy 26:1-11). Under the law an outsider who ate holy food incurred guilt (Leviticus 22:10-16), so the nations that 'devour' Israel are guilty and will suffer for it. The same logic appears in 50:7, where Israel's enemies say, 'We are not guilty, for they sinned against the LORD'. The point is double-edged: Israel's holiness protects her from the nations, but only in the LORD's own timing, not when Israel herself has broken faith.

p: Hebrew hevel, 'vapor', is Jeremiah's word for an idol.
b: Hebel is breath or vapor, the word of Ecclesiastes ('vapor of vapors'). In the prophets it names idols, things with no substance: Jeremiah 8:19; 10:3, 8, 15; 14:22. The people 'went after hebel and became hebel': they turn into what they worship (compare Psalm 115:8). The Plain English Translation uses 'empty things', and the writer of 2 Kings 17:15 quotes this line when he explains the fall of the northern kingdom.

a: who brought us up from the land of Egypt
p: No one asked the question the old creed answers.
b: 'Who brought us up from the land of Egypt' is Israel's basic confession (Exodus 20:2; Deuteronomy 26:8; Amos 2:10). The failure is not just that they sinned but that no one asked 'Where is the LORD?', not even the priests (2:8). The desert is described in the words of Deuteronomy 8:15 and 32:10: waste, pits, drought. Jeremiah's question is the opposite of the people's later mocking question, 'Where is the LORD?' (Psalm 42:3, 10).

p: The word karmel is a common noun, 'fruit-garden', before it is a mountain.
b: Karmel means a fruit garden or orchard land. Mount Carmel got its name because it was green. Jeremiah uses the common noun for the whole land in 2:7 and 4:26. The land is the LORD's own, 'my land, my inheritance' (compare Leviticus 25:23); Israel lives in it as his tenant. Wrongs like idolatry and murder 'pollute' the land (Leviticus 18:24-28; Numbers 35:33-34), which is the logic of 2:7 and 3:1-2, 9.

a: Those who held the law in their hands
p: Torah, 'instruction', was the priests' job to teach.
b: Torah means instruction, the teaching of the LORD, and also the written law. The priests were the keepers and teachers of it (Leviticus 10:11; Deuteronomy 33:10; Malachi 2:7), but Jeremiah says they handled it without knowing the LORD. To 'know' the LORD is to be in a relationship with him (Hosea 4:1, 6). Compare 8:8, where the scribes say, 'We are wise, and the law of the LORD is with us.' The Plain English Translation uses 'law' for torah where the priests' office is meant and 'teaching' where the LORD speaks of his own (6:19).

p: Cyprus and Kedar mark the farthest ends of the known world.
b: The 'Kittim' are the people of Kition on Cyprus, and later all the peoples of the western sea. Kedar is a northern Arabian tribe in the east. Together they mean 'search the whole world from west to east': nowhere will you find a nation that gave up its gods. The point is that Israel's apostasy is unmatched, because the nations' gods are not real gods (2:11) and yet the nations are loyal to them.

p: 'Glory' stands for God himself; a scribal tradition says the original was 'my Glory'.
b: Kavod, 'glory', is the visible weight and splendor of God, and here it is a name for God. Psalm 106:20 has the same thought, 'they exchanged their Glory for the image of a bull', and Paul builds on both when he says people 'exchanged the glory of the immortal God' for images (Romans 1:23). Jewish tradition lists this verse among the tiqqune soferim, 'scribes' corrections', in which the scribes are said to have softened wording: here 'my Glory' (kevodi) became 'their Glory' (kevodo). The idea is old, but no known manuscript has the other reading, so the Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew text we have.

p: Flowing spring water was the best; cisterns, when cracked, held nothing.
b: Most households in the hills of Judah drank from cisterns cut in the rock and plastered with lime to hold rainwater. A crack in the plaster let the water drain away. A spring of 'living' water (mayim chayyim), water that flows, was fresh and could not run dry. The LORD is the spring; Judah has left him for cisterns of its own making. The image comes back at 17:13, 'the LORD, the spring of living water'. In John 4:10-14 and 7:37-38 Jesus uses the same image of himself.

p: The Hebrew verb can mean 'graze', 'break' or 'shave'.
b: The verb yir'ukha can come from ra'ah, 'graze, feed on', or from ra'a', 'break'. The KJV chose 'broken the crown of thy head'. The image is of Egypt's soldiers beating Judah down. Noph is Memphis and Tahpanhes (Daphne) a frontier fortress in the eastern Delta; Judeans who fled after Gedaliah's murder went to Tahpanhes, and Jeremiah with them (43:7). The Hebrew text has a Ketiv/Qere here, only a spelling of Tahpanhes. The Greek has a different verb altogether (see the variant). Egypt had hurt Judah in the past: Neco killed Josiah at Megiddo in 609 (2 Kings 23:29-30).

p: The key Jeremiah word shuv, 'turn', first appears as Judah's 'turnings away'.
b: Meshuvot are 'turnings away', 'backslidings'. They come from shuv, 'turn, return', Jeremiah's favorite verb (over a hundred times in the book). It means both to turn away from the LORD and to turn back to him, and Jeremiah plays on the two senses, especially in 3:1-4:2. Here Judah's own turning away will be her teacher. See the note at 3:12.

p: 'Armies' may mean Israel's soldiers, the angels or the stars.
b: YHWH tseva'ot, 'the LORD of Armies', is a title of the LORD as king over all forces: the armies of Israel (1 Samuel 17:45), the angels, the stars, and everything else that obeys him. Jeremiah uses it about eighty times. Here it is joined to 'Lord GOD' (Adonai YHWH) and to 'declares' (ne'um). The Greek often has 'Almighty' (Pantokrator). The Plain English Translation keeps the translation 'of Armies' as in Isaiah, though it is not an exact rendering of tseva'ot.

p: The phrase stands for the old open-air shrines the law told Israel to destroy.
b: 'Every high hill and every leafy tree' is stock language for the Canaanite-style shrines (the 'high places') which Deuteronomy 12:2 orders destroyed, and which the books of Kings blame on nearly every king (1 Kings 14:23; 2 Kings 16:4; 17:10). Jeremiah applies to them the picture of a prostitute sprawled out (tso'ah) for any customer. This image of idolatry as adultery was Hosea's (Hosea 2:2-13; 4:12-14) and is developed in Ezekiel 16 and 23.

p: The vine is one of the Bible's pictures of Israel.
b: The soreq is a red grape vine of the best kind. Israel as the LORD's vine appears in Psalm 80:8-16, Isaiah 5:1-7 (the song of the vineyard), Hosea 10:1 and Ezekiel 15 and 19. Here the problem is not the gardener but the vine, which turned into 'spoiled shoots of a foreign vine'. The Greek has 'a foreign vine' too. Jesus calls himself 'the true vine' (John 15:1), the vine that does not fail.

p: Neter is a mineral alkali, borit a plant ash: strong cleaners that cannot clean guilt.
b: Neter is natron, a natural soda used for washing (the KJV's 'nitre' is a misleading word, since it is not saltpeter); borit is soap made from plant ashes (Malachi 3:2 'launderer's soap'). Together they were the strongest cleaners of the day. The guilt is a dye, not dirt. The Greek says 'nitre' and 'herb'.

p: The plural names the many local Baal shrines.
b: Ba'al means 'lord' or 'master', and each place had its own Baal. 'The Baals' stands for all of them (also in 9:14; Judges 2:11). The Baal cult promised rain and fertility, which is why the drought of Jeremiah 14 is a test of who gives rain (14:22). The 'valley' is often taken to be the Valley of Ben-hinnom, where children were burned (7:31; 19:5), but the text does not say so.

p: Judah is two animals driven by instinct, a she-camel and a wild donkey.
b: The two animals, a young she-camel running about and a female wild donkey sniffing the wind, picture an appetite no one can turn aside. The point is that the people run after the Baals because they cannot help themselves; they claim innocence (2:23) while their conduct, seen in the valley, shows what they do. In 2:25 they say 'No use!' and admit nothing will stop them. 'In her month they will find her' means that the female in season is easy to find: Judah's lovers need no effort to find her.

a: to a piece of wood, "You are my father,"
t: Wood is father, stone is mother
p: The sexes look reversed: the wooden pole is called father, the stone mother.
b: Wood probably means the sacred pole (asherah) or a carved idol; stone the standing pillar (matstsevah). Commentators note that the roles look reversed, since the Asherah was a goddess and the pillar was linked to the male god, and they give different explanations: the speakers confuse their own gods, the words are mocking, or the images simply stand for the family of gods. Whatever the reason, the point is the same: the people say to objects what only the LORD may be called, 'my father' (3:4, 19), and 'you gave birth to me'. Note the Ketiv/Qere: written 'me', read 'us'.

p: Each city had its own gods and shrines.
b: Archaeology shows many small shrines and figurines in Judean towns of the 700s and 600s BC. The Greek adds a second half to the verse: 'according to the number of the streets of Jerusalem they sacrificed to Baal'. The Hebrew of 11:13 has the thought in other words, 'as many as the streets of Jerusalem are the altars to Shame'. The Plain English Translation follows the shorter Hebrew here. See the variant.

p: The sense of 'You never caught them tunneling in' depends on the law of the thief.
b: The verse is hard in Hebrew. The 'tunneling' (machteret) refers to Exodus 22:2-3: a householder who killed a thief caught tunneling in at night had no bloodguilt. Jeremiah's point is probably that the poor who were killed were not thieves caught in the act, so there was no excuse for their blood on the skirts of the powerful. The pointed text reads 'you found them' (feminine, to the people); the unpointed consonants would also allow 'I found them', which is how the KJV takes it ('I have not found it by secret search'), and the Greek verb can be read that way too. The last words, ki 'al kol elleh, 'but on all these', are unclear: they may mean 'in spite of all this', or that the blood is found 'on all these' hems, or, if one reads a similar word, 'under every oak', as the Greek has it (see the variant). The Plain English Translation leaves the line open, as the Hebrew does.

a: with your hands on your head
p: Hands on the head show grief and shame, as for Tamar.
b: Putting the hands on the head was a sign of grief and shame; Tamar did it after she was assaulted by her half-brother (2 Samuel 13:19). Judah will leave Egypt, her ally, as she left Assyria, shamed. The warning was fulfilled in the reigns of Jehoiakim and Zedekiah, when Egypt promised help against Babylon and failed (37:5-10; Ezekiel 17:15-17; 29:6-7).

a: Suppose a man sends his wife away
p: Jeremiah argues from the law that forbids a man to take back a divorced wife, and then the LORD invites Israel back.
b: Deuteronomy 24:1-4 says that if a man divorces his wife, and she marries another man, her first husband may not take her back; she has been 'polluted' for him. Jeremiah uses that law as an argument: if even a human husband cannot return to such a wife, how can Israel, who has had many lovers, hope to come back? Then the LORD does what the law forbids a husband to do: 'Yet return to me.' The point is not that the law is wrong but that God's grace goes past it. The Pharisees' question about divorce in Matthew 19:3-9 also turns on Deuteronomy 24. Rashi hears the opening as the LORD saying, 'I have to tell you that you are no longer fit for me', and reads the last words as the LORD's longing for her return.

p: The land is polluted by adultery, as in Deuteronomy 24:4 the woman is 'polluted'.
b: The Greek says 'that woman' where the Hebrew has 'that land' (see the variant). The Hebrew's choice is deliberate: Deuteronomy 24:4 warns that taking back the divorced wife would 'bring sin on the land'. Jeremiah returns to the idea often: Judah's idolatry 'pollutes the land' (3:2, 9; 2:7).

p: The Hebrew says 'like an Arab', a desert herder who waits by the road.
b: The Hebrew 'aravi is 'an Arab', the word Isaiah 13:20 also uses ('no Arab will pitch his tent there'). It means a person of the desert fringe, a camel herder or caravan robber who hides along the road to waylay travelers. The Plain English Translation says 'nomad' because 'Arab' today names a very large group of peoples. The picture is of a woman sitting at the roadside, as Tamar did (Genesis 38:14), watching for customers. The Greek has 'a crow' for 'an Arab' (see the variant).

p: The drought is the covenant penalty, and the shameless forehead is the people's answer.
b: The withholding of rain is the first of the covenant curses (Deuteronomy 11:16-17; 28:23-24; Amos 4:7-8). Jeremiah ties it to the people's broken faith; chapter 14 gives a whole liturgy for a drought. A 'forehead' that cannot blush is the same as a hardened face (5:3; 6:15; Ezekiel 3:7-9). The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew idiom and glosses it.

a: in the days of King Josiah
p: The sisters oracle is dated to Josiah's reign, the time of his reform.
b: This is the only message in chapters 1-6 that Jeremiah himself dates, apart from the call. 'Israel' is the northern kingdom, which fell to Assyria in 722 BC; 'Judah' is Jerusalem's kingdom. Josiah's reform reached into the old north (2 Kings 23:15-20), and Jeremiah's call to 'turn back' toward the north (3:12) may belong to that moment, while the exiles of Israel were still alive in Assyria. His verdict on Judah's reform, that it was done 'with a lie' (3:10), is sharp, and many scholars see in it a judgment on how deep Josiah's reform went. Others think the verse is from a later editor who set the message in Josiah's reign.

p: The exile of Samaria in 722 BC is the divorce; Judah saw it and did not learn.
b: The 'certificate of divorce' (sefer keritut) is the document of Deuteronomy 24:1, 3. In the picture, the LORD divorced the northern kingdom when Assyria carried Israel off in 722 BC. Isaiah 50:1 asks where the certificate is, a way of saying that the LORD has not finally divorced Zion. Ezekiel 23 tells the same story of two sisters, Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Jerusalem), in much grosser words.

a: Turn back, Israel, who turned away
p: One Hebrew root says 'turn back', 'turn away' and 'turning away', and Jeremiah plays on it.
b: The root shuv (turn, return) appears more than a hundred times in Jeremiah. Here shuvah meshuvah Yisra'el is 'Turn back, you turning-away Israel'. Older English versions say 'backsliding Israel' (KJV); many modern ones say 'faithless Israel'. The Plain English Translation keeps the pun by using 'turn' throughout: 'turn back' (shuv), 'turned away' and 'turning away' (meshuvah, shovav). The same word is used for 'bring back the exiles' (shuv shevut, 29:14; 30:3). The word for repentance in Hebrew is the word for turning around on the road.

p: The adjective is built on hesed, 'loyal love'.
b: Hasid, 'loyal', is the adjective from hesed ('loyal love'). It is used of the LORD in this verse and in Psalm 145:17. The Plain English Translation chooses 'loyal' to keep the link with 'loyal love', since many English versions say 'merciful'. The verb behind 'hold a grudge' (natar) is the one in Leviticus 19:18 (do not 'bear a grudge'): the LORD is bound by his own law, and he does not keep a grudge forever.

p: The word for husband is also the name of the god Israel ran to.
b: Ba'al means 'master' or 'husband'. It is the same word as the name of the storm god Baal. The LORD says, in effect, 'I am your ba'al', and the pun is sharp: Israel went to the Baals, but her real husband is the LORD. Hosea says it outright: in the day of restoration, 'you will call me "my husband" (ishi) and no longer "my Baal"' (Hosea 2:16). The verb can also mean 'I have married you' or 'I have been your master'. 'One from a town and two from a clan' is a promise to gather even the few.

a: shepherds who are like my own heart
p: The promise recalls David, the man after God's heart, and prepares 23:1-6.
b: 'Shepherds' means rulers. The words 'after my own heart' recall Samuel's words to Saul, 'the LORD has sought out a man after his own heart' (1 Samuel 13:14), taken to mean David (Acts 13:22). The shepherds are to feed the people with da'at and haskel, 'knowledge and insight', the very things Jeremiah says the priests and prophets lack (2:8; 4:22). The theme comes to a head in 23:1-8 and in Ezekiel 34, and in the NT in the picture of Jesus as the good shepherd (John 10).

a: The ark of the covenant of the LORD
p: The ark vanishes from the record; later traditions say it was hidden.
b: The last time the Bible clearly places the ark in the Temple is under Josiah, who told the Levites to put it back in the house (2 Chronicles 35:3). The lists of what the Babylonians took in 586 do not mention it (2 Kings 25:13-17; Jeremiah 52:17-23). Later stories fill the gap. 2 Maccabees (a book of the Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, not of the Protestant) says that Jeremiah hid the tent, the ark and the altar of incense in a cave on the mountain where Moses saw the land, until God gathers his people again (2 Maccabees 2:4-8). The Talmud ascribes the hiding to Josiah (Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 52b). The Ethiopian Orthodox Church holds that the ark is in Aksum. These are traditions; the Bible itself does not say. Rashi explains that the people will not need the ark, since the whole assembly will be holy.

p: When the ark is gone, the whole city becomes the LORD's seat, and the nations come.
b: The ark was the footstool or throne on which the LORD sat above the cherubim (1 Samuel 4:4; Psalm 99:1). In the new age, Jerusalem itself will be that throne, and all the nations will gather to it, as in Isaiah 2:2-4 and Zechariah 8:20-23. The idea has been read in different ways. Many Jewish readers see it as a hope for a rebuilt Jerusalem; many Christians see it fulfilled in the church (Galatians 4:26; Hebrews 12:22) or in the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:2-3, 24); others look for it in a future earthly age. The Greek lacks 'to the name of the LORD, to Jerusalem' (see the variant).
r: Isaiah 2:2-4; Zechariah 8:20-23; Psalm 99:1; Galatians 4:26; Hebrews 12:22; Revelation 21:2-3

p: The people called him father in 3:4, but only to get out of trouble.
b: In 3:4 they said 'My father' while in trouble; here the LORD wants them to say it and mean it. The LORD as Israel's father is old language: Deuteronomy 32:6; Isaiah 63:16; Hosea 11:1-4. Ephraim is called his firstborn in 31:9. Jesus teaches his followers to say 'Our Father' (Matthew 6:9).

p: Scribes and prophets called Baal 'the shameful thing'.
b: Bosheth, 'shame', became a way of saying Baal without saying his name. It shows up in names: Ish-bosheth (also written Ish-baal, 1 Chronicles 8:33), Mephibosheth (Merib-baal, 1 Chronicles 8:34), Jerubbesheth (Jerubbaal, 2 Samuel 11:21; compare Judges 6:32). Jeremiah says in 11:13 that the altars to Bosheth are as many as the streets of Jerusalem. Here Shame has swallowed what the ancestors earned, including their children. The Plain English Translation capitalizes it, so readers see that a god, and not a feeling, is meant.

a: Let us lie down in our shame
p: A confession in the people's voice, spoken in advance of their return.
b: The weeping on the bare hills in 3:21 is heard by the LORD, and he supplies the words of repentance in 3:22-25, as Hosea does (Hosea 14:1-3). Is it what the people say, or what they are told to say? Most commentators treat 3:22b-25 as a model confession, the speech of a repentant Israel, which the LORD puts in their mouths in hope. The people of Jeremiah's day did not say it; the exiles, who read the book, did. It sees the whole history, 'we and our ancestors', as sin.

a: then the nations will bless themselves by him
p: The promise to Abraham reaches the nations only if Israel turns back.
b: The verb is reflexive in form, 'bless themselves', as in Genesis 22:18 and 26:4, where the nations 'bless themselves' by Abraham's offspring; in Genesis 12:3 it is passive, 'will be blessed'. Jeremiah makes the blessing depend on Israel's repentance and honest oaths, 'in truth, in justice and in righteousness': the nations will take Israel's God as the name they bless by, if Israel itself lives for him. Paul reads Genesis 12:3 as a promise of the gospel for the Gentiles (Galatians 3:8). The Greek reads the last words, 'in him they will praise God in Jerusalem'.

a: Plow up new ground for yourselves
p: Hosea gave the same command a century earlier.
b: The line is word for word in Hosea 10:12, 'Plow up new ground for yourselves, for it is time to seek the LORD'. The picture is of ground never worked, which can be sown without thorns choking the seed; Jeremiah returns to it in 12:13, 'they sowed wheat and reaped thorns'. Jesus' parable of the sower has seed falling among thorns (Matthew 13:7). The point is that repentance has to go deep, not be sown on top of an old crop of sins.

a: take away the foreskins of your hearts
p: The sign of the covenant must reach the heart.
b: To circumcise the heart is to remove what stops it from listening. Moses said, 'Circumcise your hearts' (Deuteronomy 10:16), and added that the LORD himself would one day do it (Deuteronomy 30:6). Jeremiah calls ears 'uncircumcised' in 6:10 and says in 9:25-26 that Egypt, Edom, Ammon, Moab and the desert peoples are circumcised in the flesh and Israel is uncircumcised in the heart. Paul says that true circumcision is 'of the heart, by the Spirit' (Romans 2:28-29; compare Philippians 3:3; Colossians 2:11), and Stephen charges his hearers with being 'uncircumcised in heart and ears' (Acts 7:51). Jewish readers have always taken the verse as a call to inner change, not as a rejection of the physical sign.
r: Deuteronomy 10:16; Deuteronomy 30:6; Jeremiah 6:10; Jeremiah 9:25-26; Romans 2:28-29; Acts 7:51; Colossians 2:11

a: Blow the ram's horn in the land!
p: The shofar was the alarm of war as well as of worship.
b: The shofar is the ram's horn. It was blown for the beginning of festivals and the new moon, and also as the alarm that called men to arms or warned of an enemy (Amos 3:6; Hosea 5:8; Joel 2:1). Jeremiah's poems are full of it: 4:19, 21; 6:1, 17. The only Qumran scroll that preserves this verse, 4QJer-c (4Q72), has parts of 4:5 and 4:13-16 and agrees with the Hebrew text we have, except that it has the waw of 'and blow'. That waw is the Ketiv reading of the Leningrad Codex, so the scroll is a witness for the written text against the marginal Qere. The Plain English Translation uses 'ram's horn' for shofar as in Isaiah.

p: A key word, 'break' or 'crash', is repeated all through the poems.
b: Sheber means a break: of bones (Leviticus 21:19), of a pot, of a wall, of a nation. It is the word Jeremiah returns to again and again in these poems: 4:6, 20; 6:1, 14; 8:11, 21; 10:19; 14:17; 30:12. 'Crash after crash' in 4:20 is the same word twice. The Plain English Translation uses 'crash' in all of them, so the reader can see the thread, and in 6:14 'the broken place'.
r: Jeremiah 6:1; Jeremiah 6:14; Jeremiah 8:21; Jeremiah 10:19; Jeremiah 14:17; Jeremiah 30:12

a: A lion has come up out of his thicket
p: A lion stands for the invader; the picture comes back for Babylon.
b: The lion is the king of beasts and a common picture of an invader (Nahum 2:11-13 of Nineveh). Here it is the 'nation-destroyer' that is on the road from the north. Later in the book lions stand for Israel's enemies: in 50:17 Israel is a scattered flock that lions have driven off, with Assyria the first to devour it and Nebuchadnezzar the last to gnaw its bones. The LORD himself comes like a lion from the Jordan's thickets against Edom (49:19) and Babylon (50:44). The Plain English Translation says 'broken camp' for the Hebrew nasa', which means to pull up the tent pegs and march.

a: You have truly deceived this people
p: Jeremiah appears to accuse the LORD of letting the false prophets say 'Peace'.
b: Nasha' means to deceive, to mislead. The Hebrew says 'surely you have deceived'. Rashi explains that the false prophets deceived the people and compares the serpent's word in Genesis 3:13 ('the serpent deceived me'). Other readers keep the LORD as the subject: Jeremiah is saying, in anguish, that the LORD allowed the lying prophets to speak (compare 1 Kings 22:20-23; Ezekiel 14:9). The Greek turns the line into a question ('Have you really deceived this people?'). Jeremiah returns to the charge in 20:7, 'you enticed me, LORD, and I was enticed'. The 'peace' the false prophets promised is the theme of 6:14; 8:11; 14:13; 23:17; 28:9.
r: Genesis 3:13; 1 Kings 22:20-23; Ezekiel 14:9; Jeremiah 6:14; Jeremiah 20:7; Jeremiah 23:17

p: Literally 'the daughter of my people': a loving name for the people as a whole.
b: Bat 'ammi, literally 'the daughter of my people', is a poetic name for the people seen as a young woman, like 'Daughter Zion' (4:31). Jeremiah says it often (6:26; 8:11, 19, 21-22; 9:1, 7; 14:17) and so does Lamentations (2:11; 3:48). The Plain English Translation says 'my dear people'. The scorching east wind from the desert was too hot and strong to winnow with; it carries no use, only damage.

p: Dan was the northern edge of the land; the news follows the invader's road south.
b: Dan lay at the northern end of the land, and Ephraim's hills lie between Dan and Jerusalem. The call tells of an army descending the central ridge, the road any army from the north would take. Compare Isaiah 10:28-32, where the Assyrian army comes down toward Jerusalem town by town.

p: The speaker is the prophet, or the prophet voicing God's own pain.
b: These verses are the cry of someone who is in pain for the people. Many older commentators hear Jeremiah himself. Abraham Heschel (The Prophets, 1962) described the prophet as one who shares the 'pathos' of God, and Terence Fretheim hears the voice of God in this poem and in 8:18-9:3. The book does not say, and the shifting voice may be deliberate: in Jeremiah the prophet and God both grieve. Note the Ketiv/Qere in the first line (see the variant). 'Innards' (me'ay) are the seat of feeling.

p: The vision uses the words of Genesis 1:2 to say the land has returned to chaos.
b: Tohu wabohu, 'shapeless and empty', is the state of the earth before God's work in Genesis 1:2, and the only other place the pair occurs is Isaiah 34:11. In 4:23-26 the poet looks four times (ra'iti, 'I looked') and sees creation undone: the earth without form, the heavens without their lights (Genesis 1:3, 14-18), the mountains shaking, no human being (Genesis 1:26-27), the birds gone (Genesis 1:20-22), the fruitful land a desert (Genesis 2:5-9). Michael Fishbane showed the pattern, with Job 3:3-13. The Greek says only 'and behold, nothing', so the verbal echo of Genesis is in the Hebrew alone. Whether Jeremiah borrowed from a text of Genesis 1 or both draw on a shared tradition is debated.
r: Genesis 1:2; Isaiah 34:11; Isaiah 24:1-6; Zephaniah 1:2-3; Hosea 4:3; Job 3:3-13

a: I will not make a complete end
p: The refrain limits the judgment: it will be terrible, but not total.
b: The line comes back in 5:10, 5:18, 30:11 and 46:28. It is the other side of the language of the ruined land (4:27a). The LORD promises a remnant even in the worst. For the way the judgment is also said to be unchanging, see the next verse. The Greek has this sentence in 4:27 and 5:10, 5:18 as well.

a: I have not changed my mind
t: God does not relent, and God does
p: Here the LORD will not change his mind; elsewhere the same book says he may.
b: Nicham, 'change my mind, relent', is the verb of God's regret. Here the LORD says he will not relent; in 18:7-10 and 26:3, 13 he says he will relent if the people turn; in 15:6 he says, 'I am tired of relenting'. Numbers 23:19 says God is not a man that he should change his mind, and 1 Samuel 15:11, 29, 35 uses the verb both ways in one chapter. The usual way to read these is that 4:28 is about this particular judgment, once the time for turning back is past, while 18:7-10 sets the general rule that a warning is conditional. Others see the language as showing a God who is moved.
r: Jeremiah 15:6; Jeremiah 18:7-10; Jeremiah 26:3; Numbers 23:19; 1 Samuel 15:29; Jonah 3:10

p: Jerusalem dresses as Jezebel did, for allies who now want her dead.
b: Scarlet, gold jewelry and eye paint (pu'k, kohl) are the equipment of a woman seeking lovers; Jezebel painted her eyes before Jehu came (2 Kings 9:30). The 'lovers' are Judah's political partners, Egypt and Assyria (2:18, 36) and later Babylon, who now turn against her. Ezekiel 16 and 23 develop the same picture at length, as does Lamentations 1:2, 19.

p: A city is a woman, a 'daughter', in Hebrew poetry.
b: Bat Tsiyyon, 'Daughter Zion', is the city of Jerusalem seen as a young woman, a common title in Isaiah, Micah, Lamentations and Zechariah. In poems of judgment she is in labor or in distress (Micah 4:9-10); in poems of hope she is told to rejoice (Zechariah 2:10; 9:9). The Plain English Translation keeps the title as in the earlier books. The cry here is the cry of a woman in her first labor, which is the hardest.

t: The search for one just person
p: Abraham bargained for ten at Sodom; here even one would be enough.
b: The LORD offers to forgive the whole city if one person can be found who 'acts with justice' and 'looks for faithfulness' (emunah, trustworthiness). Abraham's bargain for Sodom stopped at ten (Genesis 18:22-33); here the price is one. In Ezekiel 22:30 the LORD looks for a man to stand in the gap and finds none, and Isaiah 59:15-16 says he was shocked that no one intervened. The story is an indictment: the search of one city's streets fails. The verse is sometimes quoted as if it said that no human being anywhere is righteous, but it does not say that, and the book itself later shows people who did act with justice, such as Josiah (22:15-16) and Ebed-melech (38:7-13). Paul, in Romans 3:10-12, uses Psalm 14 for a similar point.
r: Genesis 18:22-33; Ezekiel 22:30; Isaiah 59:15-16; Psalm 14:1-3; Romans 3:10-12; Jeremiah 38:7-13

p: Sheqer, 'lie, falsehood', is one of Jeremiah's heavy words.
b: Sheqer is anything false: lies, false oaths, false worship, false prophecy. It is one of Jeremiah's favorite words: 3:10, 23; 5:2, 31; 6:13; 7:4, 8; 8:8, 10; 9:3-5; 10:14; 13:25; 14:14; 23:25-32; 27:10-16; 28:15; 29:9, 21, 31. Here it describes an oath: people say 'As the LORD lives' (compare 4:2), but they swear to a lie. The commandment is Exodus 20:7, not to take the name in vain.

a: They are only the poor ones
t: Not the poor, but the great
p: The prophet's first guess is that the poor sin through ignorance; he finds the great sin knowingly.
b: Jeremiah tries an excuse for the people, that the poor do not know the LORD's way, and then goes to 'the great ones', who must know it. They too have broken the yoke. The point is that sin here is not a matter of ignorance or hardship. It also contrasts with chapter 22, where Jeremiah praises the king who 'judged the cause of the poor and needy' (22:16).

a: a leopard crouches, watching over their towns
p: The same verb as in 1:12 is used for the leopard.
b: The verb is shoqed, 'watching, staying awake', the same as in 1:12 where the LORD 'watches over' his word. The lion, wolf and leopard are three beasts that stalk their prey; Hosea 13:7-8 uses the same trio. The LORD's watchfulness over his word turns into the leopard's watchfulness over the cities. The word-play with the almond branch, which the LORD showed Jeremiah in the beginning, is not accidental.

p: A mocking denial: 'It is not he', 'He is nothing'.
b: Lo hu means 'not he'. It could mean 'he is not the one (who acts)', 'he does nothing' or 'he does not exist'. The first two fit the rest of the verse, which says that no disaster will come. The people are not atheists; they do not think the LORD will punish. Compare Zephaniah 1:12, 'The LORD will not do good, nor will he do harm'.

a: the words in your mouth into fire
p: The prophet's word is a fire that consumes the people.
b: The prophet's words are the LORD's own, and they work. Compare 1:9, where the words were put in his mouth, and 23:29, 'Is not my word like fire?' When Jeremiah tries to hold the words back, they burn 'like a fire in my bones' (20:9). The fire consumes the people (the wood), as the army does in 5:15-17: the words and the invader are the same event.

a: a nation whose language you do not know
p: Deuteronomy's curse of an invader who speaks a strange tongue.
b: Deuteronomy 28:49-50 warned that the LORD would bring against Israel 'a nation from far away ... whose language you will not understand'. Isaiah 28:11 and 33:19 also use the idea. In 701 BC Hezekiah's officials asked the Assyrian envoy to speak Aramaic and not Hebrew, so that the people on the wall would not understand (2 Kings 18:26). A foreign tongue is a sign that the people have no common ground with their conquerors.

a: For what reason did the LORD our God do all this to us?
t: The question that the exiles will ask
p: The same question and answer appear in Deuteronomy 29 and in Jeremiah 16 and 22.
b: The question 'Why has the LORD done this?' and the answer 'Because they left the covenant and served other gods' is a standard pattern: Deuteronomy 29:24-28; 1 Kings 9:8-9; Jeremiah 16:10-13; 22:8-9. Here the answer fits the punishment: those who served foreign gods in their land will serve foreigners in another land. The verse looks forward to the time when the exiles would ask this question, and the book is meant to provide the answer.

a: I made the sand a border for the sea
p: The sea keeps to its limit; the people do not keep to theirs.
b: In creation the LORD set limits on the waters (Job 38:8-11; Psalm 104:9; Proverbs 8:29). The sea was a symbol of chaos, and its obedience to a grain-sized boundary is the point: the Creator's decree is firm, and even the sea keeps it. The people, who have a mind, do not. Compare 4:23-26, where the order of creation undoes itself.

a: the autumn and the spring rain
p: Palestine's farming depended on two rainy seasons, and Baal was said to bring them.
b: Yoreh, the early or autumn rain (October-November), softens the ground for sowing; malqosh, the late or spring rain (March-April), fills the crop before harvest (Deuteronomy 11:14). In Canaanite belief Baal, the storm god, gave the rains. Jeremiah's point, as in Elijah's drought (1 Kings 17-18), is that it is the LORD who gives them (14:22). The 'weeks fixed for harvest' are the seven weeks from the barley harvest to the wheat harvest (Deuteronomy 16:9).

p: The test of justice in the prophets is how the weak are treated.
b: The orphan, the widow and the poor are the people the law protects (Deuteronomy 10:18; 24:17-22) and the test of a king's justice in the prophets: Isaiah 1:17, 23; Jeremiah 7:6; 22:3, 16. A fat and glossy class of the rich who 'overflow in matters of evil' sit on the courts that should protect the poor. The Hebrew of the line 'to see that they succeed' means that the powerful keep orphans' cases from prospering.

a: the priests rule at their side
p: The Hebrew 'rule on their hands' is unclear; the Greek has 'clapped their hands'.
b: Yirdu 'al yedeihem is literally 'rule on their hands'. It can mean 'rule at their direction' (the priests do what the false prophets say), 'rule alongside them' (priests and prophets share power), or 'take control by their means'. The Greek has 'the priests clapped their hands', that is, applauded. The line sums up chapter 5: prophet, priest and people agree, because the lie is what they want. Compare 6:13-14 and 23:9-40.

a: In Tekoa blow the ram's horn
p: A pun on Tekoa, 'blow', and a call for Benjamin to flee south.
b: Hebrew has a pun: uvitqoa' tiq'u shofar, 'in Tekoa, tiq'u the horn'. The English cannot say 'In Tekoa tekoa'. Tekoa, about ten miles south of Jerusalem, was the home of the prophet Amos (Amos 1:1). Beth-hakkerem, 'house of the vineyard', is usually identified with Ramat Rachel, a hill between Jerusalem and Bethlehem, though Ein Kerem and a site near the Herodium have also been proposed. The people of Benjamin, whose land lay north of Jerusalem and would be hit first, are told to run south through the city toward the signals. Lachish Letter 4, written in the same war, speaks of watching for the 'signals' of Lachish; that these were fire signals is an inference, and the Plain English Translation says only 'a signal'.

p: The Plain English Translation follows the comparison reading, the less common one in recent versions; the other is 'I will destroy'.
b: The Plain English Translation takes damiti from damah I, 'to be like, compare': 'I have compared Daughter Zion to a dainty pasture' (navah, 'pasture'). This fits the shepherds with flocks in the next verse. It is the less common choice among the English versions checked: the NIV, ESV and NASB take damiti from a different root, damah II, 'to destroy, cut off', and read the line as 'the lovely and delicate one, Daughter Zion, I will destroy'; the KJV and the NRSVUE read it as a comparison, with the other reading in a footnote. The next verse works either way. The Greek reads something else again: 'your height will be removed, Daughter Zion'. The Hebrew as it stands allows both readings, so neither is certain.

p: The kings and commanders are shepherds; the troops their flocks.
b: In the ancient Near East 'shepherd' was a title for a king. The invading commanders are shepherds with flocks, their armies. The tents pitched around the city are siege camps, and 'each will graze the place under his own hand' means each commander takes his own section of the siege line. A grim reversal: the pasture is eaten by the shepherds that the city had trusted for protection. Compare 25:34-36, where Judah's own shepherds are told to wail.

p: War began with rites; the attackers believe their war is sacred.
b: Qaddeshu milchamah, 'consecrate war', refers to the rites that started a campaign: sacrifice, prayers and abstinence (1 Samuel 7:9; Joel 3:9; Micah 3:5). Isaiah 13:3 speaks of the LORD's 'consecrated ones', the foreign army he has summoned. The invaders think the war is their god's, and the prophet knows it is the LORD's. The line 'let us go up at noon' is the voice of the invaders, who attack in the heat of midday when defenders expect rest, and who then regret that the day is ending.

p: Deuteronomy forbids Israel to cut fruit trees in a siege; here the LORD orders the foreign army to do it.
b: Deuteronomy 20:19-20 forbids Israel to cut down fruit trees when it besieges a city. Here the LORD himself commands the attackers to cut trees for siege ramps and engines, and the object is Jerusalem. The siege ramp (solelah) was an earth and timber ramp built against a city wall; the best-known ancient example is the Assyrian ramp at Lachish, built in 701 BC and uncovered by archaeologists. The Babylonian siege of Jerusalem lasted from 588 to 586 (39:1-2; 52:4-6).

p: The same picture as 4:4: the covering must be cut away.
b: As the heart needs circumcising (4:4; 9:26), so do the ears. 'Uncircumcised' means covered, closed. The word of the LORD, which Jeremiah is full of (6:11), is to them an insult. Stephen uses the words against the council: 'You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears' (Acts 7:51). The problem is not in the message but in the hearing.

p: These lines come again almost word for word in 8:10-12.
b: Verses 6:13-15 are repeated in 8:10-12 with these differences in the Hebrew: 6:13 says 'from their smallest to their greatest' (with 'their'), 8:10 'from the smallest to the greatest'; 8:10 opens with a line of its own (their wives and fields given to others) that matches 6:12; 6:14 says 'my people' ('ammi) where 8:11 says 'my dear people' (bat 'ammi, literally 'the daughter of my people'); 6:15 has 'and they do not even know' (gam) where 8:12 has 'and they do not know', and 'the time I call them to account' (a verb) where 8:12 has 'the time of their accounting' (a noun). Jeremiah's book repeats lines: 6:22-24 recurs in 50:41-43, 10:12-16 in 51:15-19, and 23:19-20 in 30:23-24. Scholars debate whether the repetition shows an editor's pairing of the poems or the prophet reusing his own words for new audiences. For the point about the false prophets and priests, see 6:14 and 23:9-40.

p: The false prophets cried 'Peace', treating a broken nation as scratched.
b: Shalom means peace, well-being, wholeness. The prophets of 'peace' were the court and Temple prophets who promised that Jerusalem would be safe (23:17; 28:2-4). The 'broken place' (sheber, the 'crash' of 4:6) is the nation's wound, and they say it is healed 'as though it were a trifle'. Ezekiel 13:10 uses the same charge: they 'misled my people, saying "Peace," when there is no peace'. Micah 3:5 says the prophets cry 'Peace' for those who feed them. Paul uses the same words in 1 Thessalonians 5:3: 'When they say, "Peace and security," then destruction will come on them suddenly.'
orig: שָׁלוֹם שָׁלוֹם וְאֵין שָׁלוֹם (shalom shalom we'en shalom)
r: Ezekiel 13:10; Micah 3:5; Jeremiah 8:11; Jeremiah 23:17; Jeremiah 28:2-4; 1 Thessalonians 5:3

a: Ask about the paths of long ago
p: The call is to ask where the good road is, not to return to old customs; the people refuse.
b: A popular use takes 'the ancient paths' as a call to go back to old customs or old ways of worship. The verse does not say that. The LORD tells the people to stand at the crossroads and ask where the good road is, and to walk on it. The 'paths of long ago' (netivot 'olam) are the way of the covenant that the LORD set for Israel in the beginning (compare Deuteronomy 30:15-20; Jeremiah 18:15). Judah's answer, 'We will not walk on it', is the book's refrain of refusal, so the call is a return to the LORD, not to tradition for its own sake. Rashi's only comment on 6:16 names the Hebrew word for 'rest', marge'a. Jesus' invitation, 'you will find rest for your souls' (Matthew 11:29), uses the same words as the Hebrew here; the Greek of Jeremiah has 'purification' instead (see the variant).

p: The prophets are the watchmen who blow the alarm.
b: A watchman on the wall warned the city of danger. Ezekiel was told he was Israel's watchman and would be held accountable if he failed to blow the horn (Ezekiel 3:17-21; 33:1-9); compare Isaiah 62:6 and Habakkuk 2:1. Here the watchmen are Jeremiah and the prophets who spoke the LORD's warning, and the people's reply, 'We will not listen', is the reason their blood is on their own heads (Ezekiel 33:4).

p: The Hebrew 'edah' may be 'congregation' or 'witnesses'; the Greek has something else.
b: 'Edah usually means a congregation or assembly. Some read the vowels differently as 'edot, 'witnesses': 'know, you witnesses, what is among them'. The last words, 'et asher bam, 'what is among them', are obscure. The Greek reads 'the nations heard, and those who shepherd their flocks'. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew as written. The point is clear: the nations are called as witnesses, as in the heavens and earth in 6:19 and Isaiah 1:2.

a: Why do you bring me frankincense from Sheba
p: The offerings were lawful; they are rejected because they come with injustice.
b: Frankincense was an ingredient of the grain offering (Leviticus 2:1-2), and 'sweet cane' of the anointing oil (Exodus 30:23); both were imported from far away, Sheba being South Arabia. Chemical tests on altars at the Judahite shrine at Arad, from the 700s BC, found traces of frankincense, which shows it was in use in Judah (Arie, Rosen and Namdar). The LORD does not say that the offerings are forbidden but that he does not accept them: they come from people who do not listen to his words (6:19) and who oppress (6:6-7). Other prophets say the same: Isaiah 1:11-17; Amos 5:21-24; Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:6-8. Jeremiah 7:21-23 goes further.
r: Leviticus 2:1-2; Isaiah 1:11-17; Amos 5:21-24; Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:6-8; Jeremiah 7:21-23

a: Look, a people is coming from a northern land
p: 6:22-24 comes again in 50:41-43, now aimed at Babylon.
b: Verses 6:22-24 are repeated in 50:41-43, now aimed at Babylon, and the Plains of the two passages agree where the Hebrew is the same. The Hebrew differs in these places: 6:22 has 'from a northern land' (me'erets tsafon), 50:41 'from the north' (mitsafon); 6:22 'a great nation is roused', 50:41 'a great nation and many kings are roused'; 6:23 'he is cruel' (hu', the nation), 50:42 'they are cruel' (hemah); 6:23 ends 'against you, Daughter Zion', 50:42 'against you, Daughter Babylon'; and 6:24 reads 'we have heard the news of them, and our hands hang limp ... distress has seized us', but 50:43 'the king of Babylon has heard the news of them, and his hands hang limp ... distress has seized him'. The same description of a terrifying northern army serves first for Judah's fall and then for Babylon's. That fits the view that the 'foe from the north' was a pattern the book applied more than once. See the note at 1:14.

p: Jeremiah's slogan, later used as a name and as a taunt.
b: Magor missaviv, 'terror all around', is Jeremiah's catchphrase: it appears in 20:3, where he renames Pashhur 'Terror All Around'; in 20:10, where his enemies mock him with it; and in 46:5 and 49:29. Psalm 31:13 and Lamentations 2:22 have it too. Here it is a warning to stay inside the walls, which would not be safe.

a: a tester among my people, a fortress
p: The Hebrew has two words, 'tester' and 'fortress', and the second may be an error.
b: The Hebrew has bachon, 'tester, assayer', and mivtsar, 'fortress', the same word as in 1:18 where Jeremiah is made 'a fortified city'. Many commentators think mivtsar here stands for a word meaning 'refiner' or 'ore', since the next verses are about testing metal. The Greek has 'a tester among tested peoples'. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew words as written, which echoes 1:18: the same man is a fortress and a tester.

p: The smelter's work fails: the lead is used up, and the silver is still dross.
b: The picture is the refining of silver by cupellation, which commentators explain this way: lead is added to the molten ore and the fire is blown with bellows, so that the lead carries off the impurities and leaves pure silver. Here the lead is 'finished off by the fire' and the process still fails. The people are alloy that will not separate. The written text and the margin differ on one word in the second line, and the Greek has a different line altogether (see the variant). Compare Isaiah 1:22, 25; Ezekiel 22:17-22; Zechariah 13:9; Malachi 3:2-3, where the refining succeeds.

a: Water stays fresh in a well
p: The rare verb heqir means 'keep fresh' to some, 'pour out' to others.
b: The verb heqir (haqir in the first half) is rare, and its root is disputed. Some take it from a root meaning 'be cool, fresh': a well keeps its water fresh, and Jerusalem keeps her evil fresh, never stale and never running dry. Others take it from a root meaning 'dig, well up': a well gushes its water, and she gushes her evil. English versions divide, the ESV and NRSV with 'keeps fresh' and the NIV with 'pours out'. The Plain English Translation takes the 'fresh' sense, because the Greek (psychei, 'keeps cool') agrees, and puts it in its own words. The written text and the margin also differ on the noun, 'cistern' or 'well' (see the variant).

p: The Hebrew nefesh, often 'soul', is rendered 'yourselves' here.
b: The Hebrew says 'rest for your nefesh'. Nefesh is the whole living self, not a part that lives on after the body, so the Plain English Translation says 'yourselves'. Many older versions say 'souls', and Matthew 11:29 has 'souls' (psychais) in the Greek, translating the same Hebrew word. The rare word marge'a, 'rest', occurs only here and in Isaiah 28:12. Nothing in the Hebrew is lost by 'yourselves', but readers of Matthew should know that 'soul' there stands for the whole person.

p: Hebrew 'erets means 'earth' or 'land'; the poem may be about Judah, not the world.
b: 'Erets means both 'earth' and 'land'. English readers often hear 4:23-26 as the whole world undone. But the lines that follow speak of one country: 'the orchard land' and its cities (4:26), and the LORD says that 'the whole land' will be a desolation (4:27), using the same Hebrew word. The sky is part of the picture, yet the losses (people, birds, cities) are those of a single land. So the poem can be read as the end of the world, or as the end of Judah told in the words of the world's beginning. The Plain English Translation says 'earth' here because the 'heavens' stand beside it, and 'land' in 4:27 where the context is one country.
